summary: Describes test cases for evaluating congestion control algorithms for interactive real-time RTP media in a controlled environment. It is informational and works with the evaluation guidelines in RFC 8868.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8867 is a test plan. It describes how to build a lab for judging a congestion control algorithm meant for real-time calls, what to measure, what the network and the media source should look like by default, and eight scenarios that between them exercise most of what can go wrong. The goal is that two different implementations running these tests produce comparable results.

subtitle: Standardized lab scenarios for judging a proposed congestion control algorithm for real-time media.

tldr.problem: A proposed congestion control algorithm for real-time media has to be judged on how it behaves in a lab, and different labs would otherwise use different scenarios and report incomparable results.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a common structure for a test case, a set of recommended lab settings such as path delay, jitter, queue size and media source behaviour, and eight basic test cases covering capacity changes, multiple flows, competing TCP traffic and pause and resume.
tldr.outcome: The document is a set of evaluation guidelines for a controlled lab environment, with further test cases for wireless access links defined separately in RFC 8869.

today: RFC 8867 is an Informational document from January 2021 that no RFC obsoletes or updates. It remains the reference set of lab test cases for evaluating congestion control proposals for real-time media, with the wireless variants in RFC 8869.

sections.title: What the Test Cases Are For
sections.content:
The memo describes a set of test cases for evaluating congestion control algorithm proposals in controlled environments for real-time interactive media. It is based on the guidelines enumerated in RFC 8868 and the requirements discussed in RFC 8836. The test cases cover basic usage scenarios and are described using a common structure, which allows for additional test cases to be added to those described in the document to accommodate other topologies or the modeling of different path characteristics. They should be used to evaluate any proposed congestion control algorithm for real-time interactive media.

The terminology defined in RTP, the RTP Profile for Audio and Video Conferences with Minimal Control, RTCP Extended Report, the Extended RTP Profile for RTCP-based Feedback and Support for Reduced-Size RTCP applies.

The point of the whole exercise is comparison. A congestion control algorithm for live media has to keep a video call usable when the network under it changes, when several calls share one link, when a file download starts, or when one participant pauses their video. Each of those situations exposes a different failure mode, so the RFC works through them as separate test cases with a stated expected behaviour and a stated set of measurements.
sections.plainLanguage: Every congestion control proposal looks fine until something changes on the network. This RFC lists the changes that matter, sets up a lab for each one, and says what a good result looks like, so that proposals can be compared against each other rather than against each lab's own idea of a test.

sections.title: The Structure of a Test Case
sections.content:
All the test cases follow a basic structure, so that a new test scenario can be described without repeatedly explaining common attributes. The structure has a general description section describing the test case and its motivation; an expected behavior section describing the desired rate adaptation behavior; and a list of metrics to evaluate that behavior, giving the minimum set of metrics a proposed algorithm needs to measure, such as link utilization and media sending rate, together with the time granularity for measuring them, with a typical measurement interval of 200 ms.

Every test case also defines an evaluation testbed topology. In the example topology, S1 to Sn are traffic sources generating media traffic and using the congestion control algorithms under investigation, and R1 to Rn are the corresponding receivers. The path from source to destination is the forward path, and the path back is the backward path. The structure is described from the perspective of media-generating endpoints attached on the left-hand side, with media flowing forward and feedback and control messages flowing backward, although a test can also be set up with media in both directions. In that case, unless the test case says otherwise, the backward path is expected to introduce no congestion-related impairments and to have enough capacity for both media and feedback.

Path characteristics are given separately for the forward and backward directions, and apply to all the sources sending traffic on that path. If only one attribute is specified it is used for both directions, but unless specified the reverse path has no capacity restrictions and no path loss. The attributes are the path direction, the minimum bottleneck-link capacity, the reference bottleneck capacity used as a reference value for test cases with time-varying bottleneck capacities, the one-way propagation delay, which is the end-to-end latency along the path when network queues are empty, the maximum end-to-end jitter, the bottleneck queue type, for example tail drop, FQ-CoDel or PIE, the bottleneck queue size expressed as a queuing time in milliseconds, and the path loss ratio, which characterizes the non-congested additive losses and must describe the loss pattern or model used.

Application-related attributes describe the traffic source. They cover the media type, video or voice, the media flow direction, the number of media sources, the media codec, constant or variable bit rate, and the media source behaviour, which is the set of parameters that affect adaptation: the adaptability, meaning the options the encoder has, such as bit rate, frame rate and video resolution for video, or bit rate range, sampling rate variation and packetization interval for voice; the output variation, which for a variable bit rate encoder is the variation from the average target rate over a measurement interval; and the responsiveness to a new bit rate request, the lag between a request from the congestion control algorithm and the actual change in encoder output, which may be given in absolute time or as the next frame interval. The media content, the media timeline describing when the source is introduced and removed, and the startup behaviour, where the media starts at a defined bit rate, are also specified. A competing traffic source is described separately, with its direction, the types of sources, the number of sources of each type per direction, the congestion control used by each type, and its traffic timeline. Any attribute can have a set of values enclosed in brackets, each member treated as a different value for the same attribute, and it is desired to run separate tests for each.
sections.plainLanguage: Every test states what it is trying to provoke, what the algorithm is supposed to do about it, and what to record while it runs. The lab is described in a fixed vocabulary: path capacity, delay, jitter, queue type and size, loss, and then the media source, the competing traffic, and when each of them starts and stops.

sections.title: Recommended Evaluation Settings
sections.content:
To evaluate the performance of candidate algorithms, implementers must log enough information to visualize the metrics at a fine enough time granularity. The flow-level metrics are end-to-end delay for the congestion-controlled media flows, for example observed at the IP packet level and the video frame level; variation in sending bit rate and throughput, mainly observing the frequency and magnitude of oscillations; packet losses observed at the receiving endpoint; feedback message overhead; and convergence time, the time to reach steady state, with each occurrence of convergence during the test period presented. The transport-level metrics are bandwidth utilization and queue length, in milliseconds at the specified path capacity.

Unless a test case says otherwise, each path between a sender and receiver has a forward and backward direction, a reference bottleneck capacity of 1 Mbps, a one-way propagation delay of 50 ms, a maximum end-to-end jitter of 30 ms, a bottleneck queue type of tail drop, a bottleneck queue size of 300 ms, and a path loss ratio of 0%. Implementers are encouraged to run the experiment with the additional propagation delays, jitter models and Active Queue Management schemes such as FQ-CoDel and PIE described in RFC 8868.

For test cases involving time-varying bottleneck capacity, all capacity values are specified as a ratio with respect to a reference capacity value, so that capacity values can be scaled along with the media source rate range. There are two mechanisms for inducing path capacity variation: explicitly modifying the value of the physical link capacity, or introducing background non-adaptive UDP traffic with a time-varying traffic rate. Implementers are encouraged to run the experiments with both mechanisms for the test cases in sections 5.1, 5.2 and 5.3.

Unless otherwise specified, each test case includes media sources of two kinds. The video source uses a variable bit rate codec, with a bit rate range of 150 Kbps to 1.5 Mbps, a frame resolution of 144p to 720p or 1080p, a frame rate of 10 to 30 fps, a variation from the target bit rate of plus or minus 5% calculated over a one second period unless the test case says otherwise, and a responsiveness to a new bit rate request of 100 ms. The media content should represent a typical video conversational scenario with head and shoulder movement, and the RFC recommends the Foreman video sequence. The media startup behaviour is 150 Kbps. The audio source uses a constant bit rate codec at 20 Kbps.
sections.plainLanguage: Unless a test says otherwise, the lab is the same: a 1 Mbps bottleneck, 50 ms each way, 30 ms of jitter, a 300 ms queue, no loss, and a video source that can move between 150 Kbps and 1.5 Mbps and takes 100 ms to react to a new rate request. That way two different runs are comparable.

sections.title: The Basic Test Cases
sections.content:
Eight basic test cases are defined. In 5.1, variable available capacity with a single flow, the minimum bottleneck-link capacity between the two endpoints varies over time, which measures the responsiveness of the algorithm. It addresses the requirements that the algorithm adapt to an intermediate bottleneck, to a change in available capacity such as an interface change, a routing change or the abrupt arrival or departure of background traffic, and to a maximum media bit rate greater than the link capacity, in which case the scheme is expected to stabilize the sending bit rate close to the available bottleneck capacity. The expected behaviour is that the algorithm detects the path capacity constraint, converges to the bottleneck link's capacity, and avoids unwanted media rate oscillation when the sending rate approaches that capacity. The test runs 100 s with one video and one audio source, and the forward path capacity ratio changes at 40 s, 60 s and 80 s through the pattern in Table 1.

In 5.2, variable available capacity with multiple flows, the same idea is run with two media sources and with persistent network load from competing traffic. The flows stabilize around their maximum bit rate when the link is large enough, decrease their sending bit rate when the available capacity drops, and ramp up again when congestion disappears. This test runs to 125 s with a reference bottleneck capacity of 2 Mbps and a five-step capacity pattern.

In 5.3, congested feedback link with bi-directional media flows, real-time interactive media uses RTP, so RTCP or RTP header extensions carry the back channel. Because the link between communicating peers is often asymmetric, a peer may not receive feedback because the back channel is impaired or congested even when the forward channel is not. The test observes how the algorithm copes with the loss of feedback. The expected behaviour is that the algorithm copes with the lack of feedback and adapts to minimize the degradation of the media flows in the forward channel, and the logs are compared with a reference case in which the backward channel has no impairments.

In 5.4, competing media flows with the same congestion control algorithm, more than one media flow shares the bottleneck link and each uses the same algorithm, which is the typical case of an application sending more than one flow to the same destination over the same port. It focuses on the capacity-sharing aspect, where the previous test measured adaptability, stability and responsiveness. Three media flows are introduced at different times, so that there is still room for the second and the third saturates the link. The expected behaviour is that the flows converge to an optimum bit rate that accommodates all of them with minimum possible latency and loss.

In 5.5, round trip time fairness, multiple media flows share the bottleneck link but each has a different one-way propagation delay, at 10, 25, 50, 100 and 150 ms. The test runs 300 s. The effectiveness of the algorithm depends on how fast and fairly the competing flows converge to their steady states irrespective of the round trip time observed.

In 5.6, media flow competing with a long TCP flow, one or more media flows share the bottleneck link with at least one long-lived TCP flow, which downloads data throughout the session and is expected to have an infinite amount of data to send and receive. This is the case of a multimedia application coexisting with a large file download, and it addresses requirement 3 in Section 2 of RFC 8836. The expected behaviour is that the candidate algorithm may be able to avoid congestion collapse, and in the worst case the media stream falls to the minimum media bit rate. The test runs 120 s with a 2 Mbps reference bottleneck, a queue size of either 300 or 1000 ms, and the media starting at 5 s.

In 5.7, media flow competing with short TCP flows, the media flows share the bottleneck with ten short-lived TCP flows that resemble the on-and-off pattern of web traffic, where clients connect to a server and download a resource using several TCP connections. This is the case of a multimedia application with several browser windows active, and it addresses requirement 1.E in Section 2 of RFC 8836. Depending on the number of short TCP flows, the cross traffic appears either as a short burst flow or resembles a long-lived flow. The expected behaviour is that the algorithm avoids flow starvation during the presence of short and bursty competing TCP flows, streaming at least at the minimum media bit rate, and that after the competing flows terminate the media streams recover to their previous steady state, and at the very least avoid persistent starvation. The test runs 300 s with two media sources and a 2.0 Mbps reference bottleneck.

In 5.8, media pause and resume, several real-time media flows share the link and all reach a steady state, then one flow is paused for a moment, leaving more bandwidth for the rest. When the paused flow resumes it no longer has the same share and has to work its way back to a fair share. This matters for real-time interactive media, which consists of more than one flow and can pause and resume at any point in a session, and it addresses requirement 5 in Section 2 of RFC 8836. The expected behaviour is that the two remaining flows increase their rates and reach the maximum media bit rate while the third is paused, and that all three converge to the same original fair share when it resumes. In the setup, flow two is paused at 40 s and resumes at 60 s, and each flow runs for 119 s.
sections.plainLanguage: The eight cases cover: a link whose capacity keeps changing, the same with several calls on it, a back channel that is congested so feedback never arrives, several calls sharing one link fairly, calls with very different round trip times sharing fairly, a call beside a long file download, a call beside a burst of web traffic, and a call that pauses and comes back. Each one states what the algorithm should end up doing.

sections.title: Other Potential Test Cases
sections.content:
Three further test cases are listed as options that can help further evaluation. In media flows with priority, media flows have different priority levels. It is an extension of the test in section 5.4, run with different priority levels imposed on each flow: the first flow is assigned a priority of 2 and the remaining two a priority of 1, and the candidate algorithm must reflect those priorities, so that the first flow arrives at a steady-state rate approximately twice that of the other two. The algorithm can use a coupled congestion control mechanism, or a weighted priority scheduler for the bandwidth distribution according to the media flow priority.

In explicit congestion notification usage, all the basic test cases are run with the Explicit Congestion Notification feature enabled. The goal is to exhibit that the candidate algorithms do not fail when ECN signals are available, and with ECN signals enabled the algorithms are expected to perform better than their delay-based variants.

In multiple bottlenecks, one congestion-controlled media flow traverses a path with more than one bottleneck. The first flow competes with a second over the link between A and B, close to the sender side, and with a third over the link between C and D, close to the receiver side. The goal is to ensure the candidate algorithms work properly in the presence of multiple bottleneck links on the end-to-end path. The expected behaviour is full utilization at both bottleneck links without starving any of the three flows, and a fair share of the available bandwidth at each bottleneck. The setup uses a 2 Mbps reference bottleneck, capacity ratios of 1.0 between A and B, 4.0 between B and C and 0.75 between C and D, and one-way delays of 100 ms for the first flow and 40 ms for the other two, over a 300 s test.
sections.plainLanguage: Three more scenarios are suggested for anyone who wants to go further: giving some calls a higher priority than others, turning on the network's explicit congestion marking so the algorithm can react to a signal rather than to delay, and putting two bottlenecks on the same path so the algorithm has to cope with more than one constraint at once.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations in Section 6 of RFC 8868 and the relevant congestion control algorithms apply. The principles for congestion control are described in RFC 2914, and in particular any new method must implement safeguards to avoid congestion collapse of the Internet.

The evaluation of the test cases is intended to be run in a controlled lab environment, so the applications, simulators and network nodes ought to be well-behaved and should not impact the desired results. Proper measures must be taken to avoid leaking nonresponsive traffic from unproven congestion avoidance techniques onto the open Internet.

Wireless access links, both cellular and Wi-Fi, have their own test cases, defined in RFC 8869.
sections.plainLanguage: These tests are for a lab, not for the public Internet. The RFC is explicit that a candidate algorithm must not be allowed to send unresponsive traffic onto real networks, because that is the kind of behaviour that brings the Internet down for everyone.
